sentences.text: He tried to explain this to his mother in the kitchen and made a mess of it, because it came out as *there is a bat in the attic* and then as *no, listen*, and then as nothing, because she had gone pale at the bat and it took eleven minutes to get her off the subject of bats in the roof.
He tried it on the consultant in Porto in July and got a smile.
He got it out properly, in the end, to his grandfather, in the car, on the way back from Porto, because in a car you are side by side and nobody has to look at anybody.
He said that everybody kept talking about what he was going to lose.
He said that nobody had said a single sentence to him, in four months, about what he was going to have.
His grandfather drove for about a kilometre.
Then he said: "That's fair.

That's a fair thing to say and I've been as bad as the rest." And then, after another while: "What is it that you'll have?" Which was, Joaquim thought at the time and still thinks, an enormous question to be asked by an adult, and the first one anybody had put to him that was not about appointments.
He said he did not know yet.

He said that there was an animal in the attic that had built a complete room out of nothing but sound and had never wanted a bulb, and that he was not saying he was going to be a bat, and that he was aware of how it sounded.

His grandfather said: "Say it anyway." So Joaquim said that he had spent four months being handled by people who thought the important thing was the part going dark, and that he had started to think the important thing was going to be whatever he built instead, and that nobody could tell him anything about that because nobody in that house had ever had to build one.
They were about six kilometres outside Amarante.
His grandfather said, "Right," and put the indicator on, and pulled into a lay-by, and sat there for a bit with his hands on the wheel.
Then he said: "Retinitis pigmentosa." "What?" "That's the name of it.
I've not said it out loud since March and I've been ashamed of that for about a month." He put the car back in gear.
"It's a rotten word and I'm not fond of it.
But it's yours and you've had to carry it round on your own and that was not right of any of us." They did not talk for the rest of the way and it was a good silence.
Joaquim is twenty-six.

He has about eleven degrees of field left in the right eye and less in the left, and he works in acoustics, which everybody in his family finds either enormously moving or extremely funny depending on which of them you ask.
The attic at his grandfather's has a working bulb now.
It was done in 2019 by an electrician who was not told about anything.
Joaquim goes up there when he visits, in the evening, and does not turn it on.
